You will be working with the DAPR1 class survey data again, available at <https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2627_survey.csv>. Load the data into R before answering any questions.

This week, you will focus on the `procrast` variable, which measures how often students tend to procrastinate on tasks or responsibilities on a scale from 0 (never) to 100 (always). The neutral midpoint of this scale is 50, which represents "about half the time".

Our research question for this workshop (using a 5% significance level) is: 

> Do university students report procrastinating significantly more than the neutral midpoint of 50?


`r qbegin(qcounter())`
<!-- Q1 plot data + write summary of pattern in plot -->

Visualise the distribution of the `procrast` variable. Add a vertical or horizontal dashed line at the neutral midpoint (50) to help visualise the hypothesised mean value.

Once you have created the plot, write a few sentences that summarise what you observe. Does the bulk of the distribution appear to sit above or below 50?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Hints

You can add dashed lines to a `ggplot` using:

- `geom_vline(xintercept = [null hypothesis value], linetype = "dashed", colour = [colour])` for vertical lines
- `geom_hline(yintercept = [null hypothesis value], linetype = "dashed", colour = [colour])` for horizontal lines
:::

:::flash

TODO - Link to plotting the distribution of a single variable (histogram, density, etc.)

:::

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
sdata <- read_csv("https://uoepsy.github.io/data/dapr1_2627_survey.csv")

ggplot(sdata, aes(x = procrast)) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Procrastination Scores (0-100)")
```

The distribution of procrastination scores appears to be centred above the neutral midpoint of 50, with a peak at around 75 indicating unimodality. This suggests that students may, on average, report procrastinating more than "about half the time".

`r solend()`


`r qbegin(qcounter())`
<!-- Q2 specify hypotheses -->

Based on our research question, specify the null ($H_0$) and alternative ($H_1$) hypotheses.

Provide your answer in both plain English and mathematical symbols (using $\mu$ for the population mean). In your dissertation or research you only need one of the two, but we want you to practice both this week.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Hints

Remember that the null hypothesis always states "no difference", "no effect", or "nothing interesting going on". The alternative hypothesis should reflect the direction of our research question.
:::

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

- Null hypothesis ($H_0$): The mean procrastination score of university students does not differ from the neutral midpoint of 50.  
In symbols: $H_0: \mu = 50$

- Alternative hypothesis ($H_1$): The mean procrastination score of university students is greater than the neutral midpoint of 50.  
In symbols: $H_1: \mu > 50$
`r solend()`


`r qbegin(qcounter())`
<!-- Q3 run one-sample t-test -->

Use the `t.test()` function in R to test your hypotheses.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Hints

- The R code is `t.test([data]$[variable], mu = [value], alternative = "[direction]", conf.level = [value])`.
- The value specified in $H_0$ goes in `mu` = `[value]`.
- Alternative can either be `"two.sided"`, `"less"`, `"greater"` and it corresponds to the direction of $H_1$.
- A 95% confidence level corresponds to an alpha of .05.
:::

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

```{r}
t.test(sdata$procrast, mu = 50, alternative = "greater", conf.level = 0.95)
```

`r solend()`


`r qbegin(qcounter())`
<!-- Q4 check assumptions -->

<!-- Also added: data requirements -->

A one-sample t-test is valid if three things are satisfied:

1. Data requirement. The variable is numeric.
2. Assumption of independence. Observations are sampled independently.
2. Assumption of normality. Either the population is normally distributed or the sample size is $\geq$ 30.

Are the requirements/assumptions met for our data?


::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Hints

- Think about the study design.
- Check the sample size using `nrow()`.
- Create a QQ-plot to visually assess the normality of the `procrast` variable using `geom_qq()` and `geom_qq_line()`. Run a Shapiro-Wilk test using the `shapiro.test()` function.
:::

:::flash

TODO - Link to assumption checking flashcards (e.g. QQ-plot/Shapiro test)

:::

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

1. The variable is numeric, as you can see from the output of `glimpse()` or `str()`.

```{r}
glimpse(sdata)
```

2. Independence is assumed based on study design (one response per unique pseudonym/person).

3. Assumption of normality

```{r}
nrow(sdata)
```

The sample size is $n$ = `r nrow(sdata)`, which is well over 30, satisfying the assumption due to the Central Limit Theorem.

```{r}
ggplot(sdata, aes(sample = procrast)) +
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line() +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles")

shapiro.test(sdata$procrast)
```

The QQ-plot shows some deviation from normality, and the Shapiro-Wilk test is significant ($W = 0.96, p < .001$), leading to rejection of the null hypothesis of normality. However, the assumption of normality is met due to the large sample size.

`r solend()`


`r qbegin(qcounter())`
<!-- Q5 write up / report -->

Let's now practice how to report the results of a one-sample t-test using APA style.

First, calculate the sample mean and standard deviation of the `procrast` variable using the `summarise()` function.

Then, write up your one-sample t-test results. Your write-up should include:

- A explanation of what was tested.
- The sample mean ($M$) and standard deviation ($SD$).
- The test results in APA format: $t$([degrees of freedom]) = [t-statistic], $p$ = [p-value], [one-tailed/two-tailed].
- A final sentence to explain whether the null hypothesis was rejected and what this means in context.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Hints

This is the write-up from the lecture slides as an example:

> We wanted to find out whether college students score above the threshold for "low loneliness" on the UCLA Loneliness scale, which is 34.
At the 5% significance level, we performed a one-sided test of significance against the null hypothesis that college students' loneliness is equal to 34.
The results indicate that the mean loneliness for college students, 40.3, is significantly higher than the "low loneliness" threshold of 34 ($t$(486) = 15, $p$ < .001, one-tailed).

:::

`r qend()`
`r solbegin(show=params$SHOW_SOLS, toggle=params$TOGGLE)`

```{r}
sdata |> 
  summarise(
    M = mean(procrast, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD = sd(procrast, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
tbl <- sdata |> 
  summarise(
    M = mean(procrast, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD = sd(procrast, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
M <- tbl$M |>
  round(2)
SD <- tbl$SD |>
  round(2)

library(broom)
test <- t.test(sdata$procrast, mu = 50, alternative = "greater", conf.level = 0.95) |>
  broom::tidy()
```

> A one-sample t-test was conducted to determine whether university students report procrastinating at significantly higher levels than the 50 midpoint. The results indicated that the mean procrastination score ($M$ = `r M`, $SD$ = `r SD`) was significantly greater than 50, $t$(`r test$parameter`) = `r round(test$statistic, 2)`, $p$ < .001, one-tailed. Therefore, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that students, on average, report procrastinating more than "about half the time".

`r solend()`
